metadata.title: Does motivation towards science mediate the relationship between parental support and adolescent science achievement? A comparison of two countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for science literacy (15-year-olds) from Korea and the United States, with students nested in schools and a two-stage stratified sampling design. The authors explicitly note the “cluster and weights of the sampling design” and conduct analyses in Mplus, but they do not report the specific PISA weight variable name(s) used in the international database. Because the analysis is a moderated mediation model with bootstrapping across plausible values, the intended approach is to respect PISA’s complex design; however, the manuscript does not provide enough detail to confirm whether student sampling weights were actually applied versus only acknowledged. Analysts using the PISA 2015 International Database should apply the standard student sampling weights and replicate design (if available in the file) consistent with OECD/PISA guidance when reproducing the model.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 science domain data for 15-year-old students in Korea and the United States. The analytic sample includes students who completed the PISA 2015 science assessment and the context questionnaire; the study reports low missingness for the focal constructs (parental support, intrinsic/extrinsic motivation, self-efficacy, and ESCS) and states that missingness was handled via FIML with robust maximum likelihood (MLR). No additional task/module restrictions are described beyond the PISA science domain and the two-country comparison.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds), Korea and United States
main_findings.target_variable: Science achievement (PISA science literacy; 10 plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Moderated mediation (Mplus, bootstrapped indirect effects pooled with Rubin’s rules across 10 plausible values). Key reported effects: Parental support × Country on science achievement: B = 7.52 (SE = 2.25), β = 0.03, p = .001. Direct effect PS → SA: Korea B = 5.38 (SE = 1.71), β = 0.05, p = .002; United States B = −2.14 (SE = 1.64), β = −0.02, p = .193. Total effect PS → SA: Korea B = 10.15 (SE = 1.84), β = 0.10, p < .001; United States B = 1.13 (SE = 1.64), β = 0.01, p = .491. Indirect effects: PS → IM → SA (Korea B = 4.35, SE = 0.53, p < .001; US B = 3.08, SE = 0.41, p < .001); PS → SE → SA (Korea B = 1.59, SE = 0.28, p < .001; US B = 1.20, SE = 0.25, p < .001); PS → EM → SA (Korea B = −1.17, SE = 0.24, p < .001; US B = −1.02, SE = 0.21, p < .001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science (15-year-olds) data from Korea and the United States, the study leveraged parental support together with science intrinsic motivation, science extrinsic motivation, and science self-efficacy to explain science achievement (pooled across 10 plausible values). It found that the parental support effect on science achievement was significantly moderated by country—positive in Korea but not in the United States—and that all three motivational constructs mediated the parental support–achievement link, with intrinsic motivation and self-efficacy showing positive indirect effects while extrinsic motivation showed negative indirect effects. This indicates that strengthening autonomy-supportive parental practices that build students’ intrinsic motivation and science self-efficacy may improve science achievement, while cautioning that externally pressured or low-autonomy extrinsic motivation may undermine achievement gains, though the study remains correlational and cannot establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PISA 2015 science literacy data for 15-year-olds from Korea (n = 5581) and the United States (n = 5712) to test a moderated mediation model. Parental support predicts adolescents’ science intrinsic motivation, science extrinsic motivation, and science self-efficacy, which in turn mediate the relationship between parental support and science achievement (science literacy measured via 10 plausible values). The authors pooled estimates across plausible values using Rubin’s rules and handled missingness with FIML under robust maximum likelihood (MLR). Country moderated the parental support–science achievement relationship: parental support was positively associated with science achievement in Korea (direct PS → SA B = 5.38, p = .002; total B = 10.15, p < .001) but not in the United States (direct PS → SA B = −2.14, p = .193; total B = 1.13, p = .491). Indirect effects were positive through intrinsic motivation and self-efficacy, but negative through extrinsic motivation in both countries. Limitations include the correlational nature of PISA and incomplete reporting of whether specific PISA sampling weights/replicate weights were applied in the Mplus models.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The manuscript is an SEM-style moderated mediation analysis using Mplus (bootstrapping and PV pooling) rather than a machine-learning predictive modeling study; therefore, no ML algorithms (e.g., Random Forest/XGBoost) are evaluated and ml_techniques is intentionally empty. As a result, there are no ML performance metrics such as accuracy/AUC/RMSE for a predictive model, and the extraction focuses on the reported path coefficients and indirect/direct effects.
